snapshot.scope: Two fully read pinned SDK articles:609-line persistence and455-line scaling. No source-example execution, approved deployment, linked-world or diagram review.

groups.decision: Creation/resume examples describe custom IDs and automatic persistence, while the introduction says default memory state disappears at session end. Retain this scope tension and generated-ID limitation as unverified source behavior. Default clients and broad permission handlers are not tenant authorization; diagrams are not binary review.

Resume options and Auto routing are distinct from live model switching. Pending is acceptance only; committed preference, unclaimed pending and activating state must be measured separately. Failed switches preserve effective state; ephemeral failure events cannot substitute for durable state queries. Reset/unset language differences remain explicit.

WebSocket/HTTP polarity and runtime capability differ from model selection. BYOK must re-provide credentials, with source claims that keys are not persisted; actual secret custody is not verified. Azure endpoint/deploymentId snippet differs from BYOK baseUrl/model configuration and needs version/schema verification. Conversation/tool results/artifacts persist differently from in-memory tool state.

ID naming supports audit but is not stored ownership authorization. Creation-age deletion differs from inactivity. Disconnect releases memory while retaining disk data; irreversible delete requires approval, ownership and custody safeguards. Idiomatic disposal and deprecated destroy must not be inferred as permanent deletion.

No idle timeout by default; spawned-client timeout does not configure existing runtime. Active work is protected according to source, but behavior needs verification. Shared CLI requires application access/ID checks; prefix-only examples do not establish authoritative ownership. Persistent storage is necessary for container recovery, not proof recovery succeeded.

Compaction thresholds are tunable ratios. In-memory tools need own persistence/stateless design. No built-in locking means caller coordination; the constant-valued expiring Redis lock with unconditional deletion shows no ownership-safe atomic release or renewal and must not be deployed as verified exclusive locking. Summary links do not imply whole-source acceptance.

Per-user process, shared logical session and collaborative session patterns have different costs and isolation. Process separation alone does not show distinct home/storage; ID-prefix checks are not authoritative ownership. Serialization is required for shared writes, but Redis technology/TTL are choices. GET/compare/DEL has no shown atomic release; expiry has no renewal. Shared samples omit required empty-mode/auth/tool safeguards.

Any-node resume requires shared storage; sticky assignment may avoid shared storage at cost of load imbalance and failover design. Hash/round-robin code lacks complete empty-server/failure handling. Concurrency maps have no shown synchronized admission, activity ordering or authorization. Eviction disconnect preserves state rather than deleting it.

Ephemeral/persistent and container examples remain inert. Client-supplied resume/delete IDs lack shown ownership and tokens; model/compaction/latest-image/replica/port values are examples. Persistent mounts need actual access-mode, concurrent-state, network and recovery checks. All-interface listeners do not provide transport authentication.

Production cleanup, health/restart, persistent storage, secret management, observability and drain are recommendations; shared locking/any-node filesystem constraints are conditional requirements. No default idle timeout and single-process scaling remain explicit. Diagrams and linked guides require independent review.
